About: Orbital Velocity — Climb Higher, Go Slower

Source

Topic
Gravitation — circular orbits around a spherical planet
Simulation
Drag a satellite between the surface and beyond geostationary; watch orbital speed and period react.
Concept
A higher orbit is a slower orbit, yet the period grows dramatically longer because the orbit is far bigger.
Serves
NCERT Class 11 Gravitation — circular orbital speed v = √(GM/r), Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³, specific orbital energy E = −GM/(2r).
Misconception
"Higher orbit means more energy, so it must be moving faster." It has more total energy but less kinetic energy.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet the space station

The ISS orbits 400 km up and takes just 92 minutes to lap the Earth — that's 7.67 km/s. Press ▶ Play and watch it go round. Notice the two readouts: speed and period.

2 · Predict: raise it four times higher

Now imagine dragging the satellite from 400 km up to ~1 600 km — four times the altitude. What happens to its orbital speed?

3 · And the period?

You said the speed drops. What about the period — how long one lap takes?

4 · Drag it out — see for yourself

Grab the satellite and pull it outward. Watch the two readouts move in opposite directions: speed falls, period climbs — fast. Stop at the GPS preset and the GEO preset.

GPS (20 200 km): 3.87 km/s, ~12 hours. Geostationary (35 786 km): 3.07 km/s, exactly 24 hours — that's why the satellite hangs over one spot on Earth.

5 · The energy resolution

The specific orbital energy E = −GM/(2r) stays negative at every bound orbit and rises toward zero as the orbit grows. So a higher orbit has more total energy (less negative) — but the KE went down. The extra went into climbing out of the gravity well.

Turn on ∑ Formal in the top bar to see the equations. When Play is on the satellite keeps orbiting — try switching planets in the sidebar and see how Mars, with a fifth Earth's mass, changes everything.

01

At a glance

A satellite goes round a planet on a circular orbit. You choose the planet and the height of the orbit, and the sim shows the satellite's speed, its time for one lap and its energy.

What you'll learn

  • What sets the speed a satellite needs to stay on a circular orbit.
  • How the time for one lap depends on the size of the orbit.
  • Why the energy of a bound orbit is negative, and what it tells you.
The satellite moves along the dashed ring at height h above the surface, with its velocity along the ring.

  • Planet and orbit: the planet in the middle, the current orbit as a solid ring, and the three preset orbits (ISS, GPS, GEO) as dashed rings.
  • Satellite: the amber dot on the ring, labelled with its height h.
  • SPEED and PERIOD: two readouts in the bottom-left corner of the scene.

03

Gravity alone sets the speed of a circular orbit

A satellite on a circular orbit feels one force, the planet's gravity, and it points to the centre. So gravity is the centripetal force:

GMm/r² = mv²/r  ⟹  v = √(GM/r)
Here r is measured from the planet's centre, so r = R + h.

The satellite's own mass m cancels, so a gram and a tonne at the same radius move at the same speed. Each radius has exactly one circular-orbit speed.

For the ISS, r = 6378 + 400 = 6778 km, and Earth's GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², so v = 7.669 km/s. A bigger radius gives a smaller speed. At the GPS ring, r = 26 578 km is 3.9 times larger and v = 3.873 km/s is about half.

See itRaise the orbit to 5000 km above Earth. Watch for: Radius r at 11,378 km, a wider ring, and Speed v down to 5.919 km/s.
04

Kepler's third law links the period to the radius

One lap is a distance 2πr at speed v, so T = 2πr/v. Putting in v = √(GM/r) gives

T = 2π√(r³/GM)  ⟹  T² ∝ r³
T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, the same for every orbit around one planet.

A bigger orbit makes the lap longer in two ways: the path is longer and the satellite is slower. So T grows faster than r does.

Earth orbitrvT
ISS, h = 400 km6778 km7.669 km/s92.6 min
GPS, h = 20 200 km26 578 km3.873 km/s11.98 hr
GEO, h = 35 786 km42 164 km3.075 km/s23.93 hr

From the ISS to GEO, r grows 6.22 times and T grows 15.5 times, which is 6.223/2. The GEO period is one sidereal day, so that satellite hangs over one spot on the equator.

See itPress the GEO preset, played at 4×. Watch for: Period T at 23.93 hr, Speed v at 3.075 km/s, and the satellite creeping round the outer ring.
05

A higher orbit has more total energy but less kinetic energy

Per kilogram, the kinetic energy of a circular orbit is ½v² = GM/(2r), and the potential energy is −GM/r, which is zero at infinite distance. The total is

E = ½v² − GM/r = −GM/(2r)
So KE = −E and PE = 2E. The Readouts panel shows this E.

E is negative, which means the satellite is bound. A bigger r moves E toward zero, so a higher orbit has more total energy even though its KE is smaller.

Earth orbitKEPEE
ISS29.40−58.81−29.40
GPS7.50−15.00−7.50
GEO4.73−9.45−4.73

From the ISS to GEO, KE falls by 24.68 MJ/kg and PE rises by 49.35, so E gains 24.68. The engines must supply that gain.

See itPress the GPS preset. Watch for: Specific energy E at −7.50 MJ/kg, much closer to zero than the ISS value of −29.40, with Speed v at 3.873 km/s.
06

The planet enters through GM

Every formula above holds for any planet. The planet matters only through its GM and through its radius R, which sets r = R + h. A planet with a weaker pull needs less speed at the same height, and its laps take longer.

World, h = 400 kmGM (m³/s²)rvT
Earth3.986 × 10¹⁴6778 km7.669 km/s92.6 min
Mars4.283 × 10¹³3790 km3.362 km/s118.1 min
Moon4.900 × 10¹²2137 km1.514 km/s147.8 min

Mars has about one tenth of Earth's mass and the Moon about one eightieth, and the speeds fall to match. The Moon's satellite has the smallest orbit and the longest lap.

See itSwitch to the Moon at 400 km, played at 4×. Watch for: Speed v at 1.514 km/s, Period T at 2.46 hr, and a ring much smaller than Earth's.
07

Where it matters

  • The ISS. One lap takes 92.6 min, so the crew see about 15 or 16 sunrises a day. Gravity there is still 8.68 m/s², 88.5% of its value at the surface. The crew float because they and the station fall together.
  • GPS. A lap takes 11.98 hr, so each satellite makes two laps in about a day.
  • Geostationary satellites. At 35 786 km the period is 23.93 hr. Over the equator, that keeps the satellite above one spot, which suits TV and weather satellites with fixed dishes.
  • Air drag. A low satellite slowly loses energy to thin air. E becomes more negative, so r shrinks and v rises. The sim has no air.
  • Real orbits. The sim shows only circles. Real orbits are often ellipses, which Kepler's laws also cover.
08

Summary

In one line. On a circular orbit, gravity alone fixes one speed, one period and one energy for each radius.

Key points

  • v = √(GM/r), so a bigger orbit means a smaller speed.
  • T = 2π√(r³/GM), so T² ∝ r³ and the period grows faster than the radius.
  • E = −GM/(2r) is negative, KE = −E, and a higher orbit has a larger E but a smaller KE.
  • The satellite's mass cancels. The planet enters through GM and through R in r = R + h.

Common mix-ups

  • "A higher orbit has more energy, so the satellite moves faster." The total energy rises but the kinetic energy falls. The extra is stored as potential energy.
  • "Satellites are out of reach of gravity." At the ISS, gravity is still 88.5% of the surface value. It is what bends the path into the orbit.
  • "A heavier satellite needs a higher speed." The mass cancels in v = √(GM/r). Only M, the planet's mass, and r count.

Things to try on your own

  • On Earth, drag the satellite until Speed v reads about 5 km/s. Check that r matches GM/v².
  • Find the altitude where the period is exactly 3 hr, then predict whether it is above or below 5000 km before you look.
  • Put Mars on the GEO preset and compare its period with Earth's 23.93 hr.
